prompt.en: In a professional ZAP vulnerability report, what does the "Evidence" shown with the affected URL contain?

en: The DREAD score of the finding
The specific attack payload
The count of High, Medium and Low risks
The recommended code fix
The CWE reference for the weakness

explanation.en: The report pairs the affected URL with evidence, which is the specific attack payload (for example the <script>alert('XSS')</script> request). CWE links belong under References, risk counts under the Risk Breakdown, and fixes under Solution Recommendations.

prompt.en: Which rule for security testing does the lecture state?

en: Always get explicit, written permission and respect the agreed-upon scope
Systems outside the scope may be tested if they look clearly vulnerable
Permission is needed only for active scans run against production systems
Verbal permission is enough as long as the scope is put in writing later
Written permission is needed only once a vulnerability has been found

explanation.en: The lecture says to ALWAYS get explicit, written permission before any testing, ALWAYS define and respect the agreed-upon scope, and NEVER test systems outside it, because unauthorized security testing is a crime. Permission is required before any testing, not only before active scans.

prompt.en: Which legal references does the lecture cite for unauthorized security testing?

en: Turkey: TCK Articles 343 and 344; USA: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)
Turkey: TCK Articles 234 and 235; USA: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)
Turkey: TCK Articles 243 and 244; USA: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)
Turkey: TCK Articles 243 and 244; USA: Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)
Turkey: TCK Articles 243 and 244; USA: OWASP Top 10 compliance rules

explanation.en: The lecture cites TCK Article 243 (Unauthorized Access) and Article 244 (System Disruption) for Turkey, and the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) for the USA. CWE and the OWASP Top 10 are vulnerability references, not laws.

sets.title: Week 11: Chaos Engineering and Resilience Testing

prompt.en: In July 2024, a single software failure at CrowdStrike cost Fortune 500 companies an estimated how much in a matter of hours?

en: $540 million
$5.4 billion
$54 billion
$12.5 billion
$1.8 billion

explanation.en: The lecture cites an estimated $5.4 billion loss for Fortune 500 companies, showing that failures of complex distributed systems are a multi-billion dollar reality that traditional testing cannot anticipate.

prompt.en: According to the lecture, human error contributes to what share of preventable incidents?

explanation.en: The Hurricane Sandy slide states that human error contributes to 79% of preventable incidents; 43.3% is Amazon's reported decrease in SLA violations after GameDays.

prompt.en: Which sequence matches the timeline of Netflix's chaos engineering origin story?

en: 2008 database corruption, 2010 Chaos Monkey open-sourced, 2011 Simian Army announced, 2012 Chaos Kong created
2008 Chaos Monkey created, 2010 database corruption, 2011 Simian Army announced, 2012 open-sourced
2008 database corruption, 2010 Simian Army announced, 2011 Chaos Monkey created, 2012 open-sourced
2008 database corruption, 2010 Chaos Monkey created, 2011 Simian Army announced, 2012 open-sourced
2006 database corruption, 2008 Chaos Monkey created, 2010 Simian Army announced, 2012 open-sourced

explanation.en: After the August 2008 database corruption halted DVD shipping for three days, Netflix created Chaos Monkey in 2010, announced the Simian Army in 2011 and open-sourced it in 2012.

prompt.en: Which Simian Army tool simulates the failure of an entire AWS Availability Zone?

en: Chaos Gorilla
Latency Monkey
Chaos Kong
Security Monkey
Chaos Monkey

explanation.en: Chaos Gorilla simulates the loss of a whole AWS Availability Zone; Chaos Kong goes a step further and simulates a full AWS region failure.

prompt.en: A team wants to check that its services stay resilient when network communication becomes slow rather than failing outright. Which Simian Army tool is designed for this?

en: Chaos Monkey
Chaos Kong
Latency Monkey
Chaos Gorilla
Security Monkey

explanation.en: Latency Monkey injects artificial delays to test resilience to network degradation; Chaos Monkey instead randomly terminates production instances to test survival of instance loss.

prompt.en: How does principlesofchaos.org define Chaos Engineering?

en: Randomly breaking production systems without any hypothesis to see how users are affected
Experimenting on a system to build confidence that it can withstand turbulent conditions in production
Load testing a system to find the maximum traffic it can handle before it crashes in production
Testing a system before release to prove that it contains no defects under turbulent conditions
Simulating attacks on a system to find security vulnerabilities before they reach production

explanation.en: The quoted definition is experimenting on a system to build confidence in its capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production; the lecture also describes it as a hypothesis-driven, scientific practice.

prompt.en: In the fourth and final step of a chaos experiment, "Disprove Hypothesis", what do engineers do?

en: Inject real-world failure events such as server crashes, network partitions and CPU spikes
Restore every terminated instance and confirm that the hypothesis has been proven true
Predict that the steady state will continue in both the control and experimental groups
Systematically look for differences between the control and experimental groups to find weaknesses
Establish a measurable baseline of normal system behavior before anything is changed

explanation.en: Disproving the hypothesis means searching for differences between the control and experimental groups to expose weaknesses; defining a baseline, predicting that steady state continues and injecting failures are steps 1, 2 and 3.

prompt.en: In the lecture's payment-microservice example, which statement is the steady state hypothesis?

en: Inject real-world failure events into the checkout service and then record its error rate
Terminate 30% of the checkout service instances while the service is handling normal load
The checkout service must never fail, no matter how many of its instances are terminated
Auto-scaling and load balancing restore the checkout service within 30 seconds of the failure
Under normal load, the checkout service keeps p99 latency under 200ms and an error rate below 0.1%

explanation.en: A steady state hypothesis is a measurable, quantifiable description of normal behavior (p99 latency under 200ms, error rate below 0.1%); terminating 30% of instances is the experiment, and recovery within 30 seconds is the expected result.

prompt.en: A team is ready to run its first chaos experiment in production. Following the principle of minimizing the blast radius, which target should it start with?

en: An entire service
A full AWS region
A single container
Every pod in the cluster
One Availability Zone

explanation.en: The blast radius grows from container to instance/pod, service, Availability Zone and region, and teams should begin with the smallest possible blast radius in production, so a single container comes first.

prompt.en: What is the purpose of automated stop conditions (circuit breakers) in chaos experiments?

en: To halt an experiment if the system deviates too far from steady state
To widen the blast radius automatically after each successful run
To measure how long the system runs before its next failure occurs
To move an experiment from production back into a staging environment
To randomly terminate production instances during an experiment

explanation.en: Circuit breakers are a control mechanism for the blast radius: they automatically stop an experiment when the system strays too far from its steady state.

prompt.en: Which statement about the modern chaos engineering toolkit (2023-2025) is correct?

en: LitmusChaos is a CNCF project best suited to Kubernetes environments
AWS FIS is an open-source tool known as the original chaos tool
Chaos Monkey is a commercial SaaS tool aimed at enterprise adoption
Gremlin is a CNCF project with native Kubernetes (K8s) integration
Azure Chaos Studio is a commercial SaaS tool known for GameDays

explanation.en: LitmusChaos is the CNCF project with native K8s integration; Gremlin is the commercial SaaS tool known for being user-friendly and for GameDays, while Chaos Monkey is the original open-source tool.

prompt.en: A service runs on average 200 hours before it fails and then takes on average 2 hours to restore. Using the formula from the lecture, what is its MTBF?

en: 100 hours
200 hours
400 hours
198 hours
202 hours

explanation.en: MTBF = MTTF + MTTR, so 200 hours + 2 hours = 202 hours; 200 hours on its own is only the MTTF.

prompt.en: Which resilience metric answers the question "How long can a system be expected to run before it fails?"

en: p99 latency
MTTF (Mean Time to Failure)
MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)
Error rate
MTTR (Mean Time to Recovery)

explanation.en: MTTF measures how long a system runs before it fails; MTTR measures how quickly service is restored after a failure, and MTBF is the total time from one failure to the next.

prompt.en: According to the industry benchmark for MTTR given in the lecture, elite teams restore service in under how much time?

en: 60 minutes
30 minutes
5 minutes
30 seconds
15 minutes

explanation.en: The benchmark is under 30 minutes for top teams and under 5 minutes for elite teams.

prompt.en: A system offering 99.99% availability ("four nines") allows approximately how much downtime per year?

en: 5.26 minutes
8.76 hours
44 minutes
52.56 minutes
4.4 minutes

explanation.en: Four nines means 52.56 minutes of annual downtime (about 4.4 minutes per month); 8.76 hours per year corresponds to three nines and 5.26 minutes to five nines.

prompt.en: What key result did Amazon report after implementing GameDays?

en: A 43.3% decrease in mean time to recovery
A 79% decrease in preventable incidents
A 50% decrease in deployment failures
A 43.3% decrease in SLA violations
A 30% decrease in p99 latency

explanation.en: Amazon's dedicated 2-4 hour GameDay periods led to a 43.3% decrease in SLA violations; 79% is the share of preventable incidents attributed to human error.

prompt.en: What distinguishes Google's DiRT (Disaster Recovery Testing) program from the other industry approaches described in the lecture?

en: It randomly terminates production instances to test instance loss
It provides native Kubernetes integration as a CNCF project
It runs automated chaos experiments continuously in production
It sets aside dedicated 2-4 hour periods for teams to run experiments
It goes beyond technology to test business processes and human response

explanation.en: DiRT, founded in 2006 by Site Reliability Engineers, also tests business processes and human response; continuous automated chaos in production describes Netflix, and 2-4 hour periods describe Amazon's GameDays.

prompt.en: In the Honeycomb case study on an AWS Availability Zone failure, when did the team intentionally run its production experiment?

en: Only after a real AZ outage, to confirm the cause
During a maintenance window, with users logged out
During peak traffic, for a realistic test
Before any staging tests, to save rollout time
During off-peak hours, to avoid customer impact

explanation.en: Honeycomb ran staging tests first, then progressed to production and intentionally ran the experiment during peak traffic for a realistic test, terminating a third of its 'Shepherd' pods with zero customer impact.

prompt.en: Which statement reflects the core principles of resilient engineering presented in the lecture?

en: Reducing MTTR is often more valuable than trying to prevent all failures
Experiments should stay manual and separate from the CI/CD pipeline
Preventing all failures is more valuable than reducing recovery time
Experiments should start with the largest blast radius to learn the most
Technical tools alone are enough; no cultural change is required

explanation.en: The lecture states that reducing MTTR is often more valuable than trying to prevent all failures; it also says to start with a small blast radius, pair tools with cultural transformation and automate experiments in CI/CD.

sets.title: Week 12: CI/CD Pipelines and Docker for Testing

prompt.en: In the lecture, Docker is introduced as the tool that solves which universal problem?

en: The 'it works on my machine' problem
The 'slow code review' problem
The 'merge conflicts on main' problem
The 'too many manual releases' problem
The 'flaky end-to-end tests' problem

explanation.en: Docker solves the 'it works on my machine' problem by ensuring consistency everywhere, while CI/CD pipelines are described as the engine for automating software delivery.

prompt.en: A team's pipeline automatically packages every successfully tested build and delivers it to a staging environment, but a person must approve each release to production. Which practice is this?

en: Continuous Deployment
Smoke testing
Infrastructure as Code
Continuous Integration
Continuous Delivery

explanation.en: Continuous Delivery extends CI by delivering tested builds to staging and keeps a manual gate before production; Continuous Deployment removes that gate and deploys every passing change to production without human intervention.

prompt.en: What is the stated goal of Continuous Integration (CI)?

en: Validate the full system in a production-like staging environment
Perform a basic health check right after each deployment
Automatically deploy every passing change directly to production
Find and fix integration bugs early and quickly through frequent commits
Keep code deployable at all times, with a manual gate before production

explanation.en: In CI developers commit frequently and each commit triggers a build and tests, with the goal of finding integration bugs early; keeping code deployable behind a manual gate is the goal of Continuous Delivery.

prompt.en: Which order matches the stages of a CI/CD pipeline?

en: Build → Source → Test → Deploy → Staging
Source → Build → Test → Staging → Deploy
Test → Source → Build → Staging → Deploy
Source → Test → Build → Staging → Deploy
Source → Build → Staging → Test → Deploy

explanation.en: Code is committed to version control (Source), compiled or packaged (Build), validated by automated tests (Test), deployed to pre-production for final validation (Staging) and then released to users (Deploy).

prompt.en: In the test pyramid used for pipeline testing, what is the approximate distribution of tests?

en: Unit ~33%, Integration ~33%, E2E ~33%
Unit ~10%, Integration ~20%, E2E ~70%
Unit ~70%, Integration ~20%, E2E ~10%
Unit ~20%, Integration ~70%, E2E ~10%
Unit ~50%, Integration ~30%, E2E ~20%

explanation.en: Unit tests form the wide base (~70%, fast and cheap, run first), integration tests the middle (~20%) and E2E tests the small top (~10%, slow and expensive but highest confidence).

prompt.en: A new release has just been deployed and the team wants a basic health check to confirm it is working. Which test type does the pipeline testing table assign to this Deploy stage?

en: E2E tests
Linting and static analysis
Integration tests
Smoke tests
Unit tests

explanation.en: Smoke tests run at the Deploy stage as a basic health check after deployment; E2E tests belong to the Staging stage, where the full system is validated in a production-like environment.

prompt.en: Which benefit of Docker for testing refers to running tests in a clean, pristine environment every time, eliminating interference?

en: Fail Fast
Consistency
Isolation
Scalability
Caching

explanation.en: Isolation gives every test run a clean environment; Consistency means identical environments for development, testing and production, and Scalability means spinning up containers on demand for parallel tests.

prompt.en: Which statement correctly compares containers with virtual machines?

en: Containers share the host kernel, while each VM runs a full guest OS
Containers carry hypervisor overhead, while VMs run at near-native speed
Containers give hardware-level isolation, VMs process-level isolation
Containers are gigabytes in size, while VMs are only megabytes
Containers start in minutes, while VMs start in a few seconds

explanation.en: Containers share the host kernel, start in seconds, are megabytes in size, run at near-native speed and isolate at process level; VMs run a full guest OS on a hypervisor, start in minutes, are gigabytes in size and isolate at hardware level.

prompt.en: In Docker terminology, what is an image?

en: A tool for defining and running multi-container applications
A runnable, isolated instance created from a read-only template
A text file with instructions for building the application package
A public registry for storing and sharing application packages
A read-only template containing the application and its environment

explanation.en: An image is a read-only template (the 'class definition' or blueprint); a container is a runnable, isolated instance of it, a Dockerfile is the recipe that builds it and Docker Hub is the registry that stores and shares it.

prompt.en: A tester needs to start a web application, its database and a cache together as one multi-container setup. Which Docker concept is designed for this?

en: docker exec
Docker Compose
Docker image
Dockerfile
Docker Hub

explanation.en: Docker Compose is the tool for defining and running multi-container applications (the 'orchestra conductor' for your services); a Dockerfile only holds the instructions to build one image.

prompt.en: After installing Docker, which command runs a built-in container whose successful run confirms that the installation is complete?

en: docker pull nginx
docker --version
docker build -t hello-world .
docker ps -a
docker run hello-world

explanation.en: The second verification step, docker run hello-world, runs the built-in "hello-world" container; docker --version only checks which Docker version is installed.

prompt.en: Which Docker command lists all containers, both running and stopped?

en: docker rmi
docker images
docker ps -a
docker ps
docker logs -f

explanation.en: docker ps -a lists all containers whether running or stopped; plain docker ps lists only running containers, and docker images lists local images.

prompt.en: In the Python test Dockerfile, why are requirements.txt copied and the dependencies installed before the rest of the application code is copied?

en: To make the final image read-only before the tests start
For better caching of the dependency installation step
Because COPY . . would otherwise delete installed packages
So that pytest runs automatically while the image is built
Because WORKDIR can only be set after pip has finished

explanation.en: The Dockerfile comment says dependencies are copied and installed first for better caching; the rest of the code is copied afterwards with COPY . .

prompt.en: What does the instruction CMD ["pytest", "-v", "--html=report.html"] do in the Python test Dockerfile?

en: Selects the lightweight base image to start from
Installs pytest and the other listed dependencies
Runs pytest once while the image is being built
Defines the command that runs when the container starts
Sets the working directory inside the container

explanation.en: CMD defines the command to run when the container starts, so docker run my-python-tests executes pytest; RUN pip install installs the dependencies, WORKDIR sets the directory and FROM picks the base image.

prompt.en: Which statement about Jenkins, GitLab CI and GitHub Actions is correct?

en: Jenkins is self-hosted and highly configurable, with a steeper learning curve
Jenkins is built into GitHub and is best suited to open-source projects
GitHub Actions is best for complex enterprise needs and maximum control
GitHub Actions is self-hosted and configured with a Groovy Jenkinsfile
GitLab CI supports Docker only through plugins and is the easiest to learn

explanation.en: Jenkins is self-hosted, highly configurable, supports Docker via plugins and has the steeper learning curve, suiting complex enterprise needs; GitHub Actions is built into GitHub, is the easiest to learn and suits GitHub-hosted and open-source projects.

prompt.en: A project is hosted on GitLab and will use GitLab CI. Which file defines its pipeline configuration?

en: .gitlab-ci.yml
.gitlab/workflows/ci.yml
Dockerfile
.github/workflows/*.yml
Jenkinsfile

explanation.en: GitLab CI is configured with .gitlab-ci.yml; Jenkins uses a Groovy-based Jenkinsfile and GitHub Actions uses YAML files under .github/workflows/.

prompt.en: In a GitHub Actions workflow file, which key specifies the virtual machine environment for a job (for example ubuntu-latest)?

en: steps
uses
runs-on
on
services

explanation.en: runs-on selects the virtual machine environment for the job; on defines the triggering event, services spins up other containers such as a database, and steps lists the sequence of tasks.

prompt.en: A team reorders its pipeline so that the quickest checks, unit tests and linting, run before the slower test suites. Which best practice is this?

en: Environment Consistency
Parallelize
Monitor Metrics
Cache Dependencies
Fail Fast

explanation.en: Fail Fast means running the quickest tests (unit, linting) first; Parallelize means running multiple test suites simultaneously using matrix builds or test sharding.

prompt.en: What outcome did Etsy achieve after adopting robust CI/CD pipelines, Infrastructure as Code and fully integrated automated testing?

en: It grew from a few deployments per day to 50+ deploys per hour
It grew from a few deployments per year to 50+ deploys per day
It cut deployments to one per quarter in order to reach zero downtime
It grew from one deployment per week to thousands of deploys per day
It grew from a few deployments per month to 5+ deploys per day

explanation.en: Etsy went from a few deployments per year to 50+ deploys per day with near-zero downtime and faster bug detection; 'thousands of code changes daily' describes Netflix.

sets.title: Week 13: Formal Verification: Bridging Proofs and Testing

prompt.en: Which statement expresses the fundamental insight of the lecture about testing and formal verification?

en: Testing proves correctness; formal verification estimates how often bugs occur
Testing proves the absence of bugs; formal verification shows their presence
Testing and formal verification both prove the absence of all possible bugs
Testing finds design flaws; formal verification finds only coding errors
Testing shows the presence of bugs; formal verification proves their absence

explanation.en: Testing runs a finite set of inputs, so it can reveal bugs but not rule them out, while formal verification constructs a mathematical proof that they are absent. The reversed statement swaps the two roles.

prompt.en: Exhaustively testing a 64-bit processor requires 2^64 (about 18 quintillion) test cases. At 1 billion tests per second, approximately how long does the lecture say this would take?

en: About 635 years
About 18 years
About 64 years
About 6,350 years
About 2,048 years

explanation.en: The state space explosion example states that 2^64 test cases at 1 billion tests per second would take approximately 635 years, which is why exhaustive testing is infeasible.

prompt.en: In the argument for why testing isn't enough, what does the "needle in a haystack" problem refer to?

en: Static analysis tools report many bugs that turn out not to be real
Proof assistants need a human to guide every step of a proof
Properties must be written in temporal logic before they can be checked
Critical bugs lurk in rare combinations of concurrent events and timing conditions
The number of test cases grows exponentially with the size of the input

explanation.en: The needle-in-a-haystack problem is about rarity: critical bugs hide in rare combinations of concurrent events, fault scenarios and timing conditions, and at millions of requests per second such "extremely rare" events happen regularly. Exponential growth of test cases is the separate state space explosion problem.

prompt.en: Which statement correctly contrasts testing and formal verification?

en: Testing constructs a mathematical proof; formal verification runs a finite set of inputs
Testing covers only the tested cases; formal verification covers all possible inputs and states
Testing can prove the absence of bugs; formal verification can only prove their presence
Testing covers all possible inputs and states; formal verification covers only the proven cases
Testing covers design and implementation; formal verification focuses only on the implementation

explanation.en: Testing runs a finite set of inputs, so its coverage is the tested cases only, while formal verification constructs a proof covering ALL possible inputs and states. It is formal verification, not testing, whose scope covers both design and implementation.

prompt.en: On the formal methods spectrum of rigor, which pairing of technique and computational complexity is correct?

en: Theorem proving: polynomial
SMT solving: PSPACE-complete
Model checking: PSPACE-complete
Static analysis: undecidable
Model checking: NP-complete

explanation.en: The spectrum lists static analysis as polynomial, model checking as PSPACE-complete and theorem proving as undecidable, with SMT solving (NP-complete) as the enabling technology. NP-complete belongs to SMT solving, not model checking.

prompt.en: In model checking, how are the system and the properties to be checked expressed?

en: System as source code; properties as unit test assertions
System in temporal logic; properties as a finite-state machine
System in formal logic; properties as a correctness certificate
System as a finite-state machine; properties in temporal logic
System as random inputs; properties as minimal counterexamples

explanation.en: Model checking takes a system model (a finite-state machine) and properties written in temporal logic; the tool then explores all reachable states and returns either a proof or a counterexample.

prompt.en: In LTL, □ means "always", ◇ means "eventually", → means "implies" and ¬ means "not". Which formula states "Every request eventually gets a response"?

en: □(request → ◇response)
□(¬request → ◇response)
◇(request → □response)
□(response → ◇request)
◇(request → ◇response)

explanation.en: □ applied to (request → ◇response) says that at every point, a request implies that a response eventually follows. Starting the formula with ◇ instead would require this at only some single point, not for every request.

prompt.en: In theorem proving, what role does the machine (the proof assistant) play?

en: It generates random inputs and shrinks any failing case
It finds the whole proof automatically with no human input
It verifies every step of a proof that a human guides
It automatically explores every reachable state of the model
It approximates program behavior without running the code

explanation.en: Theorem proving is interactive: a human guides the proof construction and the machine acts as a meticulous assistant that verifies each step, producing a correctness certificate. Automatically exploring all reachable states describes model checking.

prompt.en: Which strength does theorem proving offer that distinguishes it from model checking?

en: It produces concrete counterexamples
It requires little expertise to use
It always runs in polynomial time
It is fully automated from end to end
It can handle infinite state spaces

explanation.en: Theorem proving handles infinite state spaces and offers the strongest guarantees, while model checking suffers from state space explosion in large systems. Full automation and concrete counterexamples are model checking's strengths, whereas theorem proving is labor-intensive and needs significant expertise.

prompt.en: Which static analysis technique is described as safely approximating program behavior?

en: Bounded checking
Abstract interpretation
Type systems
Data flow analysis
Symbolic execution

explanation.en: Abstract interpretation safely approximates program behavior. Symbolic execution runs the program with symbolic instead of concrete values, data flow analysis tracks how data moves through programs, and type systems catch errors at compile time.

prompt.en: A team wants a fully automated technique that finds bugs without running the code and scales to a very large codebase. They can accept occasional reports of bugs that aren't real. Which approach fits best?

en: Model checking
Property-based testing
Theorem proving
Exhaustive testing
Static analysis

explanation.en: Static analysis finds bugs without running code, is automated and scales to very large codebases, at the cost of possible false positives (reporting bugs that aren't real). Model checking is also automated but is limited by system scale.

prompt.en: A team needs deep, foundational verification and is willing to build proofs interactively with a proof assistant. Which tool from the verification toolbox fits?

en: Coq
TLA+
SPIN
Z3
Alloy

explanation.en: Coq (INRIA, France) is the proof assistant for deep, foundational verification. TLA+ and SPIN are model checkers, Alloy does bounded checking for software design, and Z3 is an SMT solver used as a backend for many tools.

prompt.en: Which statement about Amazon's use of TLA+ is correct?

en: A 939-line DynamoDB spec found no bugs, confirming its design
A 102-line EBS spec found only 2 subtle bugs in the service
An 804-line S3 spec found 3 bugs, one with a 35-step trace
A 939-line DynamoDB spec found 3 bugs, one with a 35-step trace
Amazon reports that engineers need 1-2 months to learn TLA+

explanation.en: The 939-line DynamoDB spec found 3 bugs, including one with a 35-step trace that would be "nearly impossible" to find via testing. The 804-line S3 spec found 2 bugs, the 102-line EBS spec found 3, and Amazon says engineers learn TLA+ in 2-3 weeks.

prompt.en: A developer tests a buggy reverse function with the property `for any list x, reverse(reverse(x)) == x`. After generating random inputs, the framework finds one that fails. What does a property-based testing framework do next?

en: Rewrites the property as a temporal logic formula and rechecks it
Explores all reachable states to prove that the failure is real
Shrinks it to the smallest input that still reproduces the bug
Issues a correctness certificate covering all the passing inputs
Reports it as a false positive and keeps generating new inputs

explanation.en: Property-based testing defines a property, generates hundreds or thousands of random inputs, and on failure shrinks to a minimal counterexample: the smallest possible input that reproduces the bug.

prompt.en: The Intel Pentium FDIV bug (1994) occurred in roughly 1 in 9 billion random divisions and led to a $475 million recall. What was the underlying flaw?

en: A 64-bit float converted to a 16-bit signed integer, causing overflow
5 missing entries in a 2,048-cell lookup table of the division unit
A deadlock between concurrent floating-point division operations
Software reused from an older chip without being re-verified for it
A rounding error in 1 of every 2,048 floating-point divisions

explanation.en: The floating-point division unit returned incorrect results because 5 entries were missing from a 2,048-cell lookup table. The 64-bit-to-16-bit conversion overflow is the Ariane 5 bug, not the Pentium bug.

prompt.en: What was the bug behind the Ariane 5 Flight 501 explosion (1996)?

en: Five missing entries in a lookup table produced wrong floating-point divisions
A 64-bit float for velocity overflowed when converted to a 16-bit signed integer
A 16-bit signed integer for velocity lost precision when converted to a 64-bit float
A 32-bit altitude value overflowed when converted to an 8-bit unsigned integer
A deadlock between two guidance processes stopped all velocity updates

explanation.en: A 64-bit float representing velocity was converted to a 16-bit signed integer; the value was larger than 32,767 and overflowed, leading to a software exception, guidance system failure and self-destruct. Missing lookup-table entries describe the Pentium FDIV bug.

prompt.en: What lesson does the lecture draw from the Ariane 5 Flight 501 failure?

en: Software that worked on Ariane 4 could safely be reused without further checks
Floating-point hardware must be checked against lookup tables before launch
The bug could only have been found by flight testing the real rocket
Reused software must be re-verified; static analysis could have detected the bug
The bug was detectable only by theorem proving, not by static analysis

explanation.en: The software was reused from the slower Ariane 4 without re-verifying it for Ariane 5's faster trajectory, so the lesson is that reuse requires re-verification. Post-accident analysis showed the bug was detectable by static analysis.

prompt.en: Which statement about industries where formal methods are standard practice is correct?

en: NASA uses the Coq proof assistant as its standard theorem prover for aerospace work
ISO 26262, via its DO-333 supplement, allows formal methods as an alternative to testing for avionics
DO-178C, via its DO-333 supplement, allows formal methods as an alternative to testing for avionics
DO-178C is the automotive functional safety standard for brake control and steering
Hardware design adopted formal methods as standard practice because of the Ariane 5 explosion

explanation.en: In aerospace, DO-178C (via the DO-333 supplement) allows formal methods as an alternative to testing for avionics, and NASA uses the PVS theorem prover. ISO 26262 is the automotive standard, and hardware design has used formal methods since the Pentium bug.

prompt.en: According to the lecture's key insights, how do testing and formal verification fit into a mature engineering process?

en: Both are necessary parts of the process, since they serve different goals
Testing alone is sufficient as long as enough random inputs are generated
Property-based testing fully replaces both unit testing and formal verification
Formal verification replaces testing once a proof of correctness exists
Formal verification is too costly to use outside academic research projects

explanation.en: Under the "tale of two goals" insight, testing finds bugs while verification proves correctness, and both are necessary parts of a mature engineering process. Formal methods are also used daily at Amazon, Microsoft, Intel and NASA, so they are not limited to research.

prompt.en: A developer wants to start applying formal thinking right away with the smallest learning investment. Which option from the recommended learning path fits, with its approximate learning time?

en: Design modeling with Alloy, about 1 day
Property-based testing with Hypothesis for Python, about 1-2 months
TLA+ for distributed systems, about 1 week
Deep verification with Coq via Software Foundations, about 2-3 weeks
Property-based testing with Hypothesis for Python, about 1 day

explanation.en: The learning path recommends property-based testing (Hypothesis for Python) to start now, with about 1 day of learning. Alloy design modeling takes about 1 week, TLA+ about 2-3 weeks and Coq via Software Foundations about 1-2 months.

sets.title: Kitap Bölüm 1: A Perspective on Testing

prompt.en: A designer forgets a required behavior, so the design document lacks something that should be present. What does the book call the resulting flaw in that document?

en: A spurious result
A fault of commission
A failure
An incident
A fault of omission

explanation.en: A fault is the representation of an error; when something that should be present is missing, it is a fault of omission, whereas entering something incorrect is a fault of commission. The book adds that faults of omission are the more difficult type to detect and resolve.

prompt.en: Which statement about failures matches the book's definition?

en: A failure occurs when a fault executes, and failures only occur in an executable representation
A failure is the symptom that alerts the user that something has gone wrong
The failure definition relates failures only to faults of omission
A failure is the representation of an error in a work product such as a design
A failure is the mistake a person makes while writing the code

explanation.en: A failure occurs when a fault executes, and failures only occur in an executable representation (usually source code or loaded object code). The symptom that alerts the user is an incident, and the definition relates failures only to faults of commission, not omission.

prompt.en: In the book's progression of terms (error, fault, failure, incident), what is an incident?

en: The execution of a fault in an executable representation
The act of exercising software with test cases
The symptom associated with a failure that alerts the user to its occurrence
A mistake made by a person, such as a coding mistake
The representation of an error in some mode of expression

explanation.en: When a failure occurs it may not be readily apparent, so an incident is defined as the symptom associated with a failure that alerts the user (or customer or tester) to it. The execution of a fault is the failure itself.

prompt.en: According to the book, a test has two distinct goals. What are they?

en: To isolate faults or to resolve faults
To find failures or to demonstrate correct execution
To prevent errors or to improve the development process
To plan tests or to evaluate test results
To find errors or to measure code coverage

explanation.en: A test is the act of exercising software with test cases, and its two distinct goals are to find failures or to demonstrate correct execution. Isolating and resolving faults are later life-cycle phases, and improving the process is the concern of SQA.

prompt.en: Poston summarizes the testing life cycle of Figure 1.1 as Putting Bugs IN, Finding Bugs, and Getting Bugs OUT. Which phases make up Getting Bugs OUT?

en: Coding, testing, and fault resolution
Test planning, test case development, and running test cases
Testing, fault classification, and fault isolation
Fault classification, fault isolation, and fault resolution
Requirements specification, design, and coding

explanation.en: The first three phases (requirements specification, design, coding) put bugs in, the testing phase finds them, and the last three phases (fault classification, isolation, resolution) get them out. Fault resolution is itself another opportunity for errors, since a deficient fix can break formerly correct software.

prompt.en: According to the book, the inputs of a test case are really of two types. Which two?

en: Preconditions and postconditions
Valid inputs and invalid inputs
Preconditions and actual inputs
Postconditions and actual outputs
Test case ID and purpose

explanation.en: Inputs are preconditions (circumstances that hold prior to test case execution) and the actual inputs identified by some testing method. Postconditions and actual outputs are the two types of expected outputs.

prompt.en: Knowing the expected output is often the hard part of a test case. What is the industrial response that the book calls Reference Testing?

en: Deriving the expected outputs directly from the program's source code
Comparing outputs with the execution history recorded for each test case
Re-running earlier test cases after a fix to catch newly broken behavior
Postulating an oracle who knows all the answers for every test case
Testing the system in the presence of expert users who judge whether outputs are acceptable

explanation.en: In Reference Testing the system is tested in the presence of expert users, who judge whether the outputs of executed test inputs are acceptable. Postulating an oracle that knows all the answers is the academic response, not the industrial one.

prompt.en: Map the statement "we have left undone that which we ought to have done, and we have done that which we ought not to have done" onto the Venn diagram of specified (S) and programmed (P) behaviors. Which mapping is correct?

en: Left undone = specified but not programmed (omission); done but ought not = programmed but not specified (commission)
Left undone = programmed but not specified (commission); done but ought not = specified but not programmed (omission)
Left undone = the intersection of S and P; done but ought not = behaviors outside both S and P
Left undone = specified but not programmed (commission); done but ought not = programmed but not specified (omission)
Left undone = behaviors outside both S and P; done but ought not = the intersection of S and P

explanation.en: Specified behaviors that were never programmed are faults of omission, and programmed behaviors that were never specified are faults of commission. The intersection of S and P is the "correct" portion, behaviors that are both specified and implemented.

prompt.en: In Figure 1.4 (S = specified, P = programmed, T = test cases; regions numbered 1–8), which regions hold specified behaviors for which no test cases exist?

en: Regions 1 and 4
Regions 2 and 5
Regions 2 and 6
Regions 4 and 7
Regions 3 and 7

explanation.en: Regions 2 and 5 lie inside S but outside T (region 2 is also programmed, region 5 is not), and their existence means testing is necessarily incomplete. Regions 1 and 4 are the specified behaviors that are tested, and regions 2 and 6 are the programmed behaviors that are not tested.

prompt.en: In Figure 1.4 (S = specified, P = programmed, T = test cases), what does region 7 represent?

en: Behaviors that are specified and tested but were never programmed
Behaviors that are programmed and tested but were never specified
Behaviors that are specified, programmed, and tested
Behaviors that are tested but are neither specified nor programmed
Behaviors that are specified and programmed but not tested

explanation.en: Region 7 lies only in T: the book lists it among test cases for unspecified behaviors (regions 3 and 7) and for unprogrammed behaviors (regions 4 and 7). A test case for unspecified behavior means either the test case is unwarranted or the specification is deficient.

prompt.en: According to the book, which two problems do functional test cases frequently suffer from?

en: Frequent identification of unspecified behaviors, compounded by heavy reliance on code reading
Dependence on the program's internal structure, compounded by use only at the unit level
Reliance on linear graph theory, compounded by an inability to use the specification
Loss of usefulness when the implementation changes, compounded by a late start after coding
Significant redundancies among test cases, compounded by possible gaps of untested software

explanation.en: Functional test cases often have significant redundancies among them, compounded by possible gaps of untested software. Their stated advantages are the opposite of a late start and loss of usefulness: they stay useful when the implementation changes and can be developed in parallel with it.

prompt.en: Which claim does Edward Miller make in defense of structural testing?

en: Statement coverage at 100% tends to find twice the defects of intuitive testing
Branch coverage at 85% or better tends to find twice the defects of intuitive testing
Branch coverage at 50% tends to find as many defects as intuitive testing
Branch coverage at 75% or better tends to find three times the defects of intuitive testing
Path coverage at 85% or better tends to find half the defects of intuitive testing

explanation.en: Miller (1991) wrote that branch coverage, if attained at the 85% or better level, tends to identify twice the number of defects found by "intuitive" (functional) testing. Poston, on the other side of the debate, said structural testing has been wasting testers' time since the 1970s.

prompt.en: A disgruntled employee writes a payroll program with hidden logic that checks his ID and creates havoc if he is ever terminated. Which form of testing is appropriate for finding this, and why?

en: Neither approach, because a fault that executes only after termination can never be tested
Functional testing, because test cases derived from the specification will exercise the termination case
Structural testing, because the hidden logic is implemented but unspecified behavior that functional tests cannot reveal
Structural testing, because the hidden logic is specified behavior that was never implemented
Functional testing, because the hidden logic is a fault of omission that only the specification exposes

explanation.en: The hidden logic is programmed but not specified (a fault of commission that, like a virus, stays dormant until triggered), and behaviors that were implemented without being specified are never revealed by functional test cases. Only structural testing, which uses the code itself, can expose it.

prompt.en: How does the book distinguish Software Quality Assurance (SQA) from testing?

en: SQA classifies faults by severity; testing classifies faults by development phase
SQA applies only at the system level; testing applies only at the unit level
SQA measures structural coverage of code; testing checks behavior against the specification
SQA improves the product by improving the process; testing is product oriented, discovering faults in a product
SQA discovers faults in a product; testing reduces the errors endemic in the development process

explanation.en: Process is how we do something and product is its end result: SQA tries to improve the product by improving the process and is concerned with reducing errors endemic in development. Testing is more product oriented and is concerned with discovering faults in a product.

prompt.en: In Beizer's fault taxonomy by severity (Figure 1.9), how is "database corruption" classified?

en: Intolerable
Very serious
Extreme
Catastrophic
Infectious

explanation.en: Figure 1.9 lists level 8, Intolerable, as database corruption. Catastrophic (9) is system shutdown, Infectious (10) is a shutdown that spreads to others, Extreme (7) is frequent "very serious" errors, and Very serious (6) is incorrect transaction execution.

prompt.en: Which fault is placed in the correct category of the book's fault tables (Tables 1.1–1.5)?

en: Parameter mismatch (type, number): data faults
Wrong operator (< instead of ≤): computation faults
Off by one: data faults
Insufficient precision (round-off, truncation): logic faults
Incorrect loop iteration: computation faults

explanation.en: Table 1.5 lists "off by one" under data faults. Wrong operator and incorrect loop iteration are logic faults, parameter mismatch is an interface fault, and insufficient precision is a computation fault.

prompt.en: In the Waterfall-based Figure 1.10, which level of testing corresponds to preliminary design?

en: Regression testing
Unit testing
System testing
Integration testing
Structural testing

explanation.en: Requirements specification corresponds to system testing, preliminary design to integration testing, and detailed design to unit testing. The book adds that structural testing is most appropriate at the unit level and functional testing at the system level.

sets.title: Kitap Bölüm 2: Examples

prompt.en: In the improved triangle problem statement, which range conditions (c1–c3) must the sides a, b, and c satisfy?

en: Each side is a real number with 0 < side ≤ 200
Each side is an integer with 1 ≤ side ≤ 100
Each side is an integer with 1 ≤ side < 200
Each side is an integer with 1 ≤ side ≤ 200
Each side is an integer with 0 ≤ side ≤ 200

explanation.en: Conditions c1–c3 are 1 ≤ a ≤ 200, 1 ≤ b ≤ 200 and 1 ≤ c ≤ 200; the upper limit of 200 is "both arbitrary and convenient" and is reused for boundary value test cases in Chapter 5. Conditions c4–c6 are the triangle inequalities a < b + c, b < a + c and c < a + b.

prompt.en: Under the improved triangle specification, what is the output for a = 2, b = 2, c = 4?

en: NotATriangle
Scalene
Isosceles
Equilateral
Value of c is not in the range of permitted values

explanation.en: All sides are in range, but condition c6 (c < a + b) becomes 4 < 4, which is false, and if any of c4, c5, c6 fails the output is NotATriangle. Isosceles is tempting because exactly one pair of sides is equal, but the Triangle Property requires the sum of any pair to be strictly greater than the third side.

prompt.en: In the traditional (FORTRAN-like) triangle implementation, match starts at 0 and is increased by 1 if a = b, by 2 if a = c, and by 3 if b = c. Which values can match actually take?

en: 0, 1, 2, or 3 only
Any integer from 0 through 6

explanation.en: If any two of the equalities hold, the third holds too, so match is 0 (no equal pair), 1, 2 or 3 (exactly one equal pair), or 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 (all equal); 4 and 5 are impossible. For the same reason the box sequence 1, 2, 5, 6 in Figure 2.1 can never execute, because a = b and b = c force a = c (box 4).

prompt.en: Program triangle2 implements the simple triangle specification and performs no range checks. What does it output for the sides a = -3, b = -3, c = 5?

en: Value of a is not in the range of permitted values
Isosceles
Not a Triangle
Equilateral
Scalene

explanation.en: Triangle2 evaluates (a < b + c) AND (b < a + c) AND (c < a + b); the last test is 5 < -6, which is false, so IsATriangle is False and it prints "Not a Triangle". The range message belongs to triangle3, which implements the improved specification; negative sides are behavior the simple specification never addresses.

prompt.en: Which kind of complexity is the NextDate function used to illustrate?

en: Event-driven interactions typical of GUI applications
Relationships between the inputs and the correct outputs
Interactions typical of the client side of client–server systems
A mix of computation and decision making
Logical relationships among the input variables

explanation.en: The book contrasts NextDate's logical relationships among input variables with the triangle program, whose complexity is due to relationships between inputs and correct outputs. The commission problem mixes computation and decision making, and the currency converter and SATM are the GUI and client–server examples.

prompt.en: Which input violates one of NextDate's range conditions c1–c3?

en: month 7, day 31, year 1999
month 2, day 29, year 2000
month 12, day 31, year 2012
month 1, day 1, year 1812
month 1, day 1, year 1811

explanation.en: NextDate requires 1 ≤ month ≤ 12, 1 ≤ day ≤ 31 and 1812 ≤ year ≤ 2012, so year 1811 is out of range. The other inputs satisfy all three conditions, including the year bounds 1812 and 2012.

prompt.en: What should be used as the expected output for a NextDate test case of June 31, 1812?

en: The message "Value of day not in the range 1..31"
The date July 1, 1812
The message "Value of year not in the range 1812..2012"
The message "Invalid Input Date"
The date June 32, 1812

explanation.en: Every variable is within its range (31 ≤ 31 and 1812 is the lower year bound), but June 31 is an invalid logical combination. The problem statement collapses all invalid day–month–year combinations into the single message "Invalid Input Date."

prompt.en: YesterDate is the inverse of NextDate: it returns the date of the day before. Using the book's leap-year rule, what should YesterDate return for March 1, 1900?

en: March 0, 1900
February 28, 1900
The message "Invalid Input Date"
February 29, 1900
February 28, 1899

explanation.en: A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4 unless it is a century year, and century years are leap years only if they are multiples of 400. So 1900 is not a leap year (unlike 2000) and the day before March 1, 1900 is February 28, 1900.

prompt.en: In the simple NextDate1, the CASE clause for 30-day months (4, 6, 9, 11) is: if day < 30 then tomorrowDay = day + 1, else tomorrowDay = 1 and tomorrowMonth = month + 1. What does it do for month 6, day 31?

en: Sets tomorrowDay to 1 and tomorrowMonth to 7
Outputs the message "Value of day not in the range 1..31"
Asks the user to re-enter the date until it is valid
Sets tomorrowDay to 32 and leaves tomorrowMonth unchanged
Outputs the message "Invalid Input Date" and stops

explanation.en: There is no special action for day = 31, so the Else branch treats June 31 like June 30 and produces July 1, which conflicts with the specification's "Invalid Input Date" (the improved NextDate2 adds this check). NextDate1 likewise maps February 29 to March 1 without checking whether the year is a leap year.

prompt.en: In the commission problem, what is the salesperson's commission on total monthly sales of $2,000?

explanation.en: Commission is 10% on sales up to and including $1000 ($100), 15% on the next $800 ($120), and 20% on sales in excess of $1800 (0.20 × $200 = $40), for $260. Applying 15% to everything above $1000 would wrongly give $250.

prompt.en: Which statement matches the commission problem statement?

en: Commission is 20% on all sales in excess of $1,000
The salesperson must sell at least $1,000 worth of parts each month
The end of the month is signaled by a telegram showing 0 locks sold
Locks cost $30, stocks cost $45, and barrels cost $25
The salesperson can sell at most 70 locks, 80 stocks, and 90 barrels in a month

explanation.en: Production limits are 70 locks, 80 stocks and 90 barrels per month. Locks cost $45, stocks $30 and barrels $25; the salesperson must sell at least one complete rifle per month; a telegram showing -1 locks marks the end of the month; and the 20% rate applies only above $1800.

prompt.en: Which statement about the SATM (simple ATM) system is correct?

en: After three incorrect PIN entries, screen 4 is displayed and the card is kept
Transactions can be applied to checking, savings, or credit accounts
Customers can choose among four transaction types, including transfers
If the customer's PAN is not found, screen 3 asks the customer to try again
Withdrawals can be any amount because the terminal holds every bill denomination

explanation.en: The customer has three chances to enter the PIN; after three failures screen 4 appears and the card is retained, which also happens when the PAN is not found. SATM offers three transaction types (deposit, withdrawal, balance inquiry) on two account types (checking, savings), and screen 7's $10 increments imply the terminal holds only $10 bills.

prompt.en: For the Saturn windshield wiper controller, what is the wiper speed when the lever is at INT and the dial is at position 2?

en: 30 wipes per minute
6 wipes per minute
4 wipes per minute
60 wipes per minute
12 wipes per minute

explanation.en: The decision table gives OFF = 0, INT with dial 1, 2, 3 = 4, 6, 12, LOW = 30 and HIGH = 60 wipes per minute. The dial matters only when the lever is at INT.

prompt.en: A common extension of the triangle problem adds right triangles and requires the sides in increasing order (a ≤ b ≤ c). Which input is a right triangle?

explanation.en: With sides in increasing order, c is the longest side and a right triangle satisfies the Pythagorean relationship c² = a² + b²; 9 + 16 = 25 holds. The other triples fail (for example 25 + 25 = 50 ≠ 49 and 36 + 64 = 100 ≠ 81).

prompt.en: Why are event-driven applications such as the currency converter particularly vulnerable to input errors?

en: Radio buttons allow several currencies to be selected at the same time
The U.S. dollar amount may only be entered after a currency has been selected
The Clear button resets only the U.S. dollar amount, leaving stale results
Events can occur in any order, so Compute may be clicked before a country is chosen
The Quit button stays disabled until a conversion has been computed

explanation.en: Because events can occur in any order, a user could click Compute without selecting a country or without entering a dollar amount. In the actual design the radio buttons are mutually exclusive, the amount may be entered before or after the currency selection, and Clear resets the selection, the dollar amount, the equivalent amount and its label.

sets.title: Kitap Bölüm 3: Discrete Math for Testers

prompt.en: According to Jorgensen, how do discrete mathematics and graph theory divide between the main testing approaches?

en: Discrete math is more applicable to functional testing; graph theory to structural testing
Discrete math is more applicable to structural testing; graph theory to functional testing
Discrete math applies to unit testing; graph theory applies only to system testing
Both mainly model continuous behavior, as calculus does for developers
Both mainly support structural testing; functional testing needs no mathematics

explanation.en: The book states that discrete mathematics is more applicable to functional testing, while graph theory pertains more to structural testing; the reversed pairing is the tempting trap.

prompt.en: In Jorgensen's set theory section, a set can be defined in three ways. Which list gives them?

en: Giving a decision rule, computing its power set, or taking its complement
Listing its elements, drawing a Venn diagram, or stating its cardinality
Listing its elements, naming its universe of discourse, or giving a partition
Listing its elements, giving a decision rule, or constructing it from other sets
Constructing it from other sets, writing a truth table, or stating a proposition

explanation.en: A set is defined by simply listing its elements, by giving a decision rule, or by constructing it from other sets; Venn diagrams only picture sets and cardinality is a property of a set.

prompt.en: Testers often meet "untestable requirements", such as N = {t : t is a nearly equilateral triangle}. What does Jorgensen give as the usual reason such requirements cannot be tested?

en: Their decision rule refers to itself, like the Barber of Seville
They boil down to an ambiguous decision rule
Their sets are infinite and cannot be drawn as Venn diagrams
Their decision rule is always false, so the set is empty
Their elements are listed in no particular order

explanation.en: Jorgensen says the reason such requirements cannot be tested often boils down to an ambiguous decision rule (is a (50, 50, 51) triangle nearly equilateral?); self-reference is a separate problem with very little application for testers.

prompt.en: Which set is defined by the decision rule {year : 2012 ≤ year ≤ 1812}?

en: No set at all, since a decision rule may never be false
The two-element set {1812, 2012}
The empty set, because the decision rule is always false
All years from 1812 to 2012 inclusive
The set {∅}, whose only element is the empty set

explanation.en: When a set is defined by a decision rule that is always false, the set is empty; no year is both ≥ 2012 and ≤ 1812, so the rule gives ∅, which is a different set from {∅}.

prompt.en: For A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}, what is the symmetric difference A ⊕ B?

explanation.en: A ⊕ B = (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B) = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} − {3, 4} = {1, 2, 5}, the elements that are in exactly one of the sets; {1, 2} is only the relative complement A − B.

prompt.en: For A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {w, x, y, z}, how many elements does the Cartesian product A × B contain?

explanation.en: |A × B| = |A| × |B| = 3 × 4 = 12 ordered pairs <a, b> with a ∈ A and b ∈ B; 7 would come from adding the cardinalities instead of multiplying them.

prompt.en: Jorgensen says the fundamental difference between ordinary graphs and directed graphs is exactly the difference between which two notions?

en: Subsets versus proper subsets of the node set
Finite versus infinite sets of nodes
Total versus partial participation of the nodes
Union versus intersection of the edge sets
Unordered pairs (a, b) versus ordered pairs <a, b>

explanation.en: For a ≠ b, (a, b) = (b, a) but <a, b> ≠ <b, a>; the book notes that this is exactly what separates ordinary (undirected) graphs from directed graphs.

prompt.en: A partition of B is a set of subsets A1, …, An with A1 ∪ … ∪ An = B and i ≠ j ⇒ Ai ∩ Aj = ∅. Which two assurances do these two properties give testers?

en: Completeness and nonredundancy
Reflexivity and antisymmetry
Total and onto participation
Closure and associativity
Determinism and unambiguity

explanation.en: The union condition guarantees completeness (every element is in some subset) and the disjointness condition guarantees nonredundancy (no element is in two subsets).

prompt.en: The Triangle Program's universe (all triplets of positive integers) is split into equilateral, isosceles, scalene, right, and nontriangles. What problem does Jorgensen point out with this partition?

en: The right subset is empty, since no integer triplet forms a right triangle
Scalene and right are not disjoint; the triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is in both
Nontriangles lie outside the universe of discourse
A partition of a set may contain at most four subsets
The five subsets do not cover every triplet of positive integers

explanation.en: A partition needs pairwise disjoint subsets, but the 3, 4, 5 triangle is both scalene and right; the subsets still cover the whole universe, so coverage is not the issue.

prompt.en: Let A = {date : 1 January 1812 ≤ date ≤ 31 December 2012}, B = {date : 2 January 1812 ≤ date ≤ 1 January 2013}, and C = A ∪ B. How does Jorgensen classify NextDate : A → C?

en: Many-to-one and onto
One-to-one and onto
One-to-one and into
One-to-many and into
Many-to-one and into

explanation.en: Distinct dates have distinct next dates (one-to-one), but the image of A is B, a proper subset of C, so NextDate : A → C is into; NextDate : A → B is the one-to-one, onto case.

prompt.en: Which statement about function types and testing does Jorgensen make?

en: Composed chains of functions are unproblematic once each function is tested
Many-to-one functions require much more testing than one-to-one functions
Into and onto functions need exactly the same domain- and range-based tests
A one-to-one, onto function has no inverse that could serve as a cross-check
One-to-one functions require much more testing than many-to-one functions

explanation.en: The book says the into/onto distinction has implications for domain- and range-based functional testing and that one-to-one functions require much more testing than many-to-one functions; a one-to-one onto function always has an inverse usable as a cross-check.

prompt.en: In a relation R ⊆ A × B, at least one element of A does not appear in any ordered pair of R. What is R's participation with respect to A?

en: One-to-many
Partial
Into
Total
Onto

explanation.en: Participation is total if every element of A is in some ordered pair and partial otherwise (mandatory vs. optional participation); onto and into describe the same idea for the elements of B.

prompt.en: Which combination of properties defines an ordering relation R ⊆ A × A?

en: Symmetric, antisymmetric, and transitive
Symmetric and antisymmetric, but not reflexive
Reflexive, symmetric, and transitive
Reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive
Reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive

explanation.en: An ordering relation (e.g., ≥ or Ancestor of) is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, whereas an equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

prompt.en: Why do equivalence relations, and the partitions they induce, bring "great efficiency" to testing?

en: Testing one element of an equivalence class lets us assume the others behave similarly
Each element of the set must be tested once, in a fixed order
Equivalence classes can only be the empty set or the whole universe
Antisymmetry guarantees that redundant test cases are detected automatically
Overlapping classes let one test case cover several classes at once

explanation.en: Partitions and equivalence relations are interchangeable, and great efficiency follows from testing just one element of an equivalence class and assuming the remaining elements behave similarly; equivalence classes never overlap.

prompt.en: For which truth values of p and q is the IF-THEN proposition p → q false?

en: p is false and q is true
p is true and q is true
p is true and q is false
p is false and q is false
Whenever p and q have different truth values

explanation.en: The IF-THEN truth table is T, F, T, T for (p, q) = TT, TF, FT, FF, so p → q is false only when p is true and q is false; "different truth values" describes exclusive-or.

prompt.en: Which expression is logically equivalent to ¬((p → q) ∧ (q → p))?

en: p ∧ q
¬p ∧ ¬q
p ∨ q
p ↔ q
p ⊕ q

explanation.en: The truth table of ¬((p → q) ∧ (q → p)) is F, T, T, F, identical to that of p ⊕ q; the un-negated (p → q) ∧ (q → p) is the bi-conditional p ↔ q.

prompt.en: With Pr(p) = |T(p)| / |U| and U the set of the 12 months of a year, what is the probability of the proposition p(m): "m is a 30-day month"?

explanation.en: The truth set T(p) is {April, June, September, November}, so Pr(p) = |T(p)| / |U| = 4/12; 11/12 would wrongly count every month with at least 30 days.

sets.title: Kitap Bölüm 4: Graph Theory for Testers

prompt.en: While checking the incidence matrix of a graph, you find a column whose entries sum to 3. What does this tell you?

en: The node in that column is a transfer node
The node in that column has degree 3
The edge in that column belongs to a loop
The graph has exactly three components
There is a mistake, since every edge has exactly two endpoints

explanation.en: Incidence-matrix rows are nodes and columns are edges, so every column must sum to 2; checking column sums is an integrity check similar to a parity check. A node's degree is a row sum, not a column sum.

prompt.en: Why can no edges be present in the condensation graph of an ordinary (undirected) graph?

en: Condensation removes every node whose degree is greater than 1
An edge would connect two components, making them one maximal component
Condensation keeps only the isolated nodes of the original graph
Edges are omitted by convention only, to keep the drawing readable
Every condensing node is a sink node, so it has outdegree 0

explanation.en: Components are maximal sets of connected nodes, so an edge between two of them would put their nodes in one path and therefore in the same component (and edges join individual nodes, not sets of nodes). As a result, components are independent and can be tested separately.

prompt.en: A digraph has nodes n1–n7 and edges <n1, n2>, <n1, n4>, <n3, n4>, <n2, n5>, <n4, n6>; n7 has no edges. Which nodes are transfer nodes?

en: n1, n2 and n4
n5, n6 and n7
n1 and n3
n2 and n4
n4 only

explanation.en: A transfer node has indegree ≠ 0 and outdegree ≠ 0: n2 (1 in, 1 out) and n4 (2 in, 1 out). n1 and n3 are source nodes, n5 and n6 are sink nodes, and n7 is both a source and a sink, which makes it an isolated node.

prompt.en: In the adjacency matrix of a directed graph, what does the sum of the entries in a node's column give?

en: The outdegree of the node
The length of the longest path ending at the node
The indegree of the node
Always 2, since each edge has two endpoints
The degree of the node, since the matrix is symmetric

explanation.en: In a digraph, a(i, j) = 1 iff there is an edge from node i to node j, so a row sum is the outdegree and a column sum is the indegree. The matrix need not be symmetric, and the always-2 column sum belongs to the incidence matrix.

prompt.en: The reachability matrix of a digraph is computed as R = I + A + A² + … + A^k, where A is the adjacency matrix. What is k?

en: The length of the longest path in the digraph
The number of strong components in the digraph
The number of source nodes in the digraph
The cyclomatic number of the digraph
The largest indegree of any node in the digraph

explanation.en: k is the length of the longest path in D and I is the identity matrix; r(i, j) = 1 iff there is a path from node i to node j.

prompt.en: A digraph has edges n1→n2, n1→n4, n3→n4, n2→n5, n4→n6 and n6→n3. How are nodes n2 and n6 connected?

en: 1-connected: a semipath but no path exists between them
3-connected: paths lead in both directions between them
0-connected: they are not joined even by a semipath
4-connected: they lie on a common cycle
2-connected: a path leads from one of them to the other

explanation.en: The semipath n2–n1–n4–n6 exists, but there is no directed path either way (n2 leads only to n5, and the cycle n3→n4→n6→n3 never returns to n2). No degree of connectedness beyond 3 exists.

prompt.en: A digraph has nodes n1–n7 and edges n1→n2, n1→n4, n3→n4, n2→n5, n4→n6 and n6→n3. Which set of nodes is a strong component?

explanation.en: A strong component is a maximal set of 3-connected nodes; n3, n4 and n6 lie on the cycle n3→n4→n6→n3, while n1 reaches n4 but nothing returns to n1, and {n4, n6} is not maximal. Condensing the strong components always gives a loop-free directed acyclic graph (DAG).

prompt.en: How does Jorgensen's improved definition of a program graph differ from the traditional definition?

en: Nonexecutable statements such as comments become separate nodes
Edges represent data flow between variables instead of flow of control
Only decision statements become nodes; sequential statements are merged into edges
Nodes may be entire statements or statement fragments, not only whole statements
The graph becomes undirected, since control can flow in both directions

explanation.en: Traditionally every node is a program statement; the improved definition lets nodes be entire statements or statement fragments, while edges still represent flow of control. For nonexecutable statements such as comments, the simplest answer is to ignore them.

prompt.en: Finite state machine transition labels in Jorgensen follow a "numerator"/"denominator" convention. What do the two parts denote?

en: Numerator: the guard condition; denominator: the transition's priority
Numerator: the number of tokens; denominator: the number of input places
Numerator: the action performed; denominator: the event that caused it
Numerator: the source state; denominator: the destination state
Numerator: the event causing the transition; denominator: the associated action

explanation.en: The numerator is the event that causes the transition and the denominator is the action associated with it; events are mandatory, while actions are optional.

prompt.en: A marked Petri net has places (p1, p2, p3, p4, p5) with marking <1, 1, 1, 2, 0>. Transition t2 has p3 as its only input place and p4 as its only output place. What is the marking after t2 fires?

explanation.en: Firing an enabled transition removes one token from each of its input places and adds one token to each of its output places, so p3 goes from 1 to 0 and p4 from 2 to 3.

prompt.en: In an event-driven Petri net (EDPN), what is the situation called when no transition is enabled, and how can it be ended?

en: Deadlock; it ends only when the net is reset to its initial marking
Event quiescence; it ends when a token is created in a port input event place
Event quiescence; it ends when a token is removed from a data place
Petri net conflict; it ends when both conflicting transitions fire together
Conservation; it ends when a port output place receives a token

explanation.en: In an EDPN, a marking with no enabled transition is a point of event quiescence, which can be broken by creating a token in a port input event place; in a traditional Petri net the same situation is called deadlock.

prompt.en: In a StateChart, state A contains substates B (its initial substate) and C, and an edge leaves the outline of A and goes to state D. What does this edge mean?

en: The transition to D can occur only when B and C are active together
The transition to D is ambiguous and must be redrawn from B and from C
The transition to D can occur only after A has left both B and C
The transition to D can occur from either B or C
The transition to D can occur only from B, A's initial substate

explanation.en: Edges start and end on the outline of a state, and an edge from a state that contains substates refers to all of them, so A → D can occur from B or from C. This convention keeps finite state machines from looking like "spaghetti code".

prompt.en: Which definition of the length of a path fits the chapter's own usage, where every node lies on a path of length 0 with itself and A² gives the paths of length 2?

en: The number of edges in the path
The number of components the path passes through
The number of nodes in the path
The number of loops contained in the path
The sum of the degrees of the nodes on the path

explanation.en: Counting edges makes a single node a path of length 0 and the entries of A² the two-edge paths (length 2); counting nodes would give a single node length 1.

prompt.en: An undirected graph has nodes n1–n7 and edges e1 = (n1, n2), e2 = (n1, n4), e3 = (n3, n4), e4 = (n2, n5), e5 = (n4, n6). Which loop(s) are created if an edge is added between n5 and n6?

en: No loop, since n5 and n6 lie in different components
One loop: n4, n5, n6, n4
One loop: n1, n2, n5, n6, n4, n1
Two loops: n1, n2, n5, n6, n4, n1 and n3, n4, n6, n3
One loop: n3, n4, n6, n5, n3

explanation.en: Before the change the component {n1, …, n6} contains no loop, so the new edge (n5, n6) closes exactly one: n1–n2–n5–n6–n4–n1 (e1, e4, new edge, e5, e2). There is no edge n4–n5 or n3–n6, so the other loops do not exist.

prompt.en: Nodes ni and nj of a digraph are 3-connected iff a path goes from ni to nj and a path goes from nj to ni. While convincing yourself that 3-connectedness is an equivalence relation on the nodes, which justification is correct?

en: Reflexive: every node lies on some cycle, so a path leads from it back to itself
Antisymmetric: two distinct nodes can never have paths in both directions
Transitive: paths ni→nj and nj→nk give a semipath between ni and nk, which suffices
Symmetric: any path from ni to nj can be reversed into a path from nj to ni
Transitive: paths ni→nj→nk and nk→nj→ni can be chained, so ni and nk are 3-connected

explanation.en: Chaining the paths ni→nj and nj→nk, and nk→nj and nj→ni, gives paths in both directions between ni and nk, so the relation is transitive. Reflexivity comes from the path of length 0 (not every node lies on a cycle), symmetry follows because the definition already demands both directions (directed paths cannot simply be reversed), and two distinct nodes on a cycle are 3-connected, so it is not antisymmetric.

prompt.en: Using the chapter's formula V(G) = e − n + p (p = number of components), what is the cyclomatic number of a Case construct graph made of one decision node with three branches, each through its own node, all rejoining at a single end node? Use the graph as described, with no edge added from the end node back to the decision node.

explanation.en: The Case graph has n = 5 nodes, e = 6 edges and p = 1 component, so V(G) = 6 − 5 + 1 = 2. The value 3 would come from e − n + 2p, or from first adding an end-to-start edge, neither of which this question uses.

prompt.en: A digraph has nodes n1–n7 and edges n1→n2, n1→n4, n3→n4, n2→n5, n4→n6, n6→n3, plus three added edges n3→n1, n4→n5 and n5→n6; n7 is isolated. Using the chapter's formula V(G) = e − n + p (p = number of components), what is its cyclomatic number?

explanation.en: Here e = 9, n = 7 and p = 2 (the main component plus the isolated n7), so V(G) = 9 − 7 + 2 = 4; adding three edges and no nodes raised it by 3 from the original 6 − 7 + 2 = 1. The value 6 would come from e − n + 2p, which this question does not use.

prompt.en: Using the chapter's formula V(G) = e − n + p (p = number of components), the digraph with nodes n1–n7 and edges n1→n2, n1→n4, n3→n4, n2→n5, n4→n6, n6→n3 (n7 isolated) has V(G) = 6 − 7 + 2 = 1. It is extended by adding nodes n8, n9 and edges n5→n8, n8→n9. What happens to the cyclomatic number?

en: It rises to 3, because two edges were added
It falls to −1, because two nodes were added
It rises to 2, because the chain forms a new component
It falls to 0, because the chain contains no decision
It stays 1, because each added edge comes with one added node

explanation.en: Now e = 8, n = 9 and p = 2, so V(G) = 8 − 9 + 2 = 1. Each new node arrives with exactly one new edge, so e − n is unchanged, and the chain hangs off n5, so no component is added.

prompt.en: In a graph whose nodes are people and whose edges mean "socializes with", which graph concepts correspond to a person's popularity and to a hermit?

en: Column sum of the incidence matrix; a cycle
Number of components; a condensing node
Cyclomatic number; a transfer node
Degree of a node; an isolated node
Length of the longest path; a strong component

explanation.en: The chapter says a node's degree indicates its "popularity", and a node with degree 0 is isolated, like a hermit.

sets.title: Kitap Bölüm 5: Boundary Value Testing

prompt.en: What is the rationale behind boundary value testing?

en: Randomly chosen input values avoid a form of bias in testing
Inputs that are treated the same need only one test case
Errors tend to occur near the extreme values of an input variable
Values in the middle of a range exercise the most program logic
Failures usually result from two or more faults occurring together

explanation.en: The book states that errors tend to occur near the extreme values of an input variable (e.g. a loop testing < instead of <=, off-by-one counters), so boundary value analysis focuses on the boundary of the input space. Avoiding bias is the argument for random testing, and "treated the same" is the idea behind equivalence classes.

prompt.en: Boundary value analysis is based on the "single fault" assumption of reliability theory. What does this assumption say?

en: A program fails only when exactly one input variable is out of its range
Each test case can reveal at most one fault in the program under test
Every fault in a program is located near the boundary of an input variable
Failures are only rarely the result of two or more simultaneous faults
A fault in one input variable never changes the output computed from the others

explanation.en: The single fault assumption says failures rarely come from two or more simultaneous faults; this is why BVA holds all but one variable at their nominal values. Rejecting the assumption leads to worst-case testing.

prompt.en: For a function F(x1, x2) with a <= x1 <= b and c <= x2 <= d, which input pair is one of the boundary value analysis test cases?

en: <x1min+, x2min+>
<x1min, x2max>
<x1max+, x2max>
<x1min-, x2nom>
<x1nom, x2max->

explanation.en: BVA holds all but one variable at its nominal value and lets that one variable take min, min+, nom, max- and max, so <x1nom, x2max-> is one of the nine cases. Pairs with two non-nominal values belong to worst-case testing, and min- or max+ values belong to robustness testing.

prompt.en: A function has 5 independent input variables. How many test cases does boundary value analysis yield?

explanation.en: Boundary value analysis yields 4n + 1 test cases: four non-nominal values (min, min+, max-, max) for each of the n variables plus one all-nominal case, so 4 x 5 + 1 = 21. 31 is the robustness count (6n + 1) and 3125 = 5^5 is the worst-case count.

prompt.en: For the triangle problem the book takes 1 as the lower bound and, arbitrarily, 200 as the upper bound of each side, with 100 as the nominal value. Which values of side c appear in its boundary value analysis test cases (Table 5.1)?

explanation.en: BVA uses min, min+, nom, max- and max, i.e. 1, 2, 100, 199 and 200. The values 0 and 201 (min- and max+) would only appear in robustness testing.
