explanation.en: With m = 25 fixed, R(M,S) = m/s drops as s grows from 11 DD-Paths to 33 DU-Paths and 40 slices. In general, more sophisticated structural metrics result in more elements, so a functional method tends to look less effective when evaluated against more rigorous structural metrics.

prompt.en: Figure 11.3 plots the effort to identify test coverage items against the sophistication of structural methods (DD-Path, Basis Path, DU-Path, Slice). What trend does it show?

en: Effort stays roughly the same for all four methods
Effort rises steadily, lowest for DD-Paths and highest for slices
Effort falls steadily, highest for DD-Paths and lowest for slices
Effort dips at Basis Path and then rises toward slices
Effort peaks at DU-Paths and then falls for slices

explanation.en: Effort increases with sophistication; the dip at Basis Path belongs to Figure 11.2 (number of test coverage items), not to the effort plot. Unlike functional methods there is no pleasing trade-off, which shows the importance of choosing an appropriate structural coverage metric.

prompt.en: For the Insurance Premium Program (11 feasible paths), boundary value testing and strong equivalence class testing each produce 25 test cases. How many paths does each cover according to Table 11.7?

en: Boundary value 6, strong equivalence class 10
Boundary value 10, strong equivalence class 6
Boundary value 6, strong equivalence class 11
Boundary value 5, strong equivalence class 10
Boundary value 11, strong equivalence class 10

explanation.en: The 25 boundary value test cases cover only six paths (p1, p2, p7, p8, p9 and p10), while the 25 strong equivalence class test cases cover ten (p1-p10). Equal test case counts can therefore give very different path coverage.

prompt.en: Each case predicate in the Insurance Premium Program is a compound condition of the form a <= x < b. Which test sets exercise these extreme values, i.e., achieve multiple-condition coverage?

en: Only the weak (5) and the strong (25) equivalence class test cases
Every method that produces at least 25 test cases
Only the boundary value (25) and the decision table (10) test cases
Only the worst-case boundary value (273) and the hybrid (25) test cases
Only the decision table (10) test cases

explanation.en: The chapter says the only methods whose test cases exercise these extreme values are worst-case boundary value testing (273 test cases) and the hybrid approach (25 test cases). Covering all 11 paths gives statement and DD-Path coverage, but multiple-condition coverage needs these extreme values.

prompt.en: In the case study's data flow analysis of the Insurance Premium Program, how are the uses of driverAge and points classified?

en: Both are output uses (O-uses)
Both are computation uses (C-uses)
driverAge is a P-use; points is a C-use
driverAge is a C-use; points is a P-use
Both are predicate uses (P-uses)

explanation.en: The chapter states that the uses of driverAge (in the Select Case predicates) and points (in the If conditions) are both predicate uses. It calls data flow testing for this problem boring: driverAge, points and safeDrivingReduction all occur in six definition-clear du-paths.

prompt.en: Exercise 2 asks you to compute the coverage, redundancy and net redundancy metrics for a gaps-and-redundancies study. Suppose a functional method produces m = 20 test cases that traverse n = 8 of the s = 10 DD-Paths of a unit. What are C(M,S), R(M,S) and NR(M,S)?

explanation.en: C(M,S) = n/s = 8/10 = 0.80 (below 1, so there are gaps), R(M,S) = m/s = 20/10 = 2.00 and NR(M,S) = m/n = 20/8 = 2.50. Swapping R and NR confuses all elements (s) with the elements actually traversed (n).

prompt.en: Exercise 3: the Insurance Premium pseudocode does not check for driver ages under 16 or over 120; the Else clause (Case 6) catches them on path p11 = 1-2-3-29-30-31-32-33. Among the functional methods in Table 11.7, which test set exercises this path?

en: The boundary value and weak equivalence class test cases
The strong equivalence class and decision table test cases
Only the worst-case boundary value test cases
All six test sets, since p11 is a feasible path
Only the hybrid test cases

explanation.en: In Table 11.7 every method except the hybrid one covers at most p1-p10; only the 25 hybrid test cases cover p1-p11 and so reach the out-of-range Case 6 path. The worst-case boundary value test cases, despite their number (273), stop at p10.

prompt.en: Exercise 3: the Insurance Premium pseudocode does not check for driver ages under 16 or over 120; only the Else clause (Case 6) catches them. If a set of test cases never uses such an age, which structural coverage result reveals this?

en: The slices on safeDrivingReduction and ageMultiplier turn out to be identical
Path p1 is traversed many times, so the coverage C(M,S) rises above 1
Path p11 (nodes 29 and 30, Case 6) is never traversed, so path coverage is incomplete
The cyclomatic complexity V(G) of the program graph turns out to be below 11
Every DD-Path is traversed, which shows that the Case 6 branch was executed

explanation.en: Out-of-range ages take the Else clause (Case 6) on p11 = 1-2-3-29-30-31-32-33, so test cases without them leave p11 untraversed and nodes 29-30 unexecuted, and path coverage is not met. C(M,S) can never exceed 1, and V(G) = 11 is a property of the program graph, not of the tests.

sets.title: Tutorial 1: Writing Effective Test Cases

prompt.en: How does the article define a test case?

en: A group of small related cases, maybe a maximum of 10, that are executed together as one unit
A description of the application's current behavior, written down as the reference for later test runs
A document describing project objectives, priorities, milestones, schedule, risks and dependencies
Components describing input, action and an expected response, used to determine if a feature works correctly
A record of the variables and their values that the tester enters into the application under test

explanation.en: The article says a test case has components that describe input, action and an expected response to determine whether a feature works correctly, i.e. a set of instructions on HOW to validate a test objective. A group of up to about 10 small cases is the article's description of a test procedure.

prompt.en: According to the article, what is the basic objective of writing test cases?

en: To let developers skip the fixing of defects
To validate the test coverage of an application
To make ad hoc testing the main approach
To replace the functional requirements document
To record the application's current behavior

explanation.en: The article states that the basic objective of writing cases is to validate the test coverage of an application. It adds that writing cases brings standardization and minimizes the ad hoc approach, rather than encouraging it.

prompt.en: A tester has already written basic cases from the specification and user documentation and now writes cases that depend on the application's actual functional and system flow. Which level of the test writing process is this?

en: Level 5, maintenance of the regression suite
Level 1, basic cases from the available specification
Level 3, grouping cases into a test procedure
Level 4, automation of the project
Level 2, the practical stage based on the actual flow

explanation.en: The article calls Level 2 the practical stage in which writing cases depends on the actual functional and system flow of the application. Level 1 writes basic cases from the specification and user documentation, Level 3 groups cases into procedures, Level 4 is automation, and there is no Level 5.

prompt.en: According to the article, what is a test procedure?

en: A group of small test cases, maybe a maximum of 10
The automation script produced in the final level of test writing
The list of variables and their values used by one test case
A single atomic step that has no further sub-steps
The plan describing documentation standards, change control and acceptance criteria

explanation.en: The article defines the test procedure as nothing but a group of small cases, maybe a maximum of 10, written at Level 3 of the test writing process. Automation is Level 4, and the list of variables and their values is the test data field.

prompt.en: A test case contains the entry "User Name = Administrator, Password = admin2015". In the article's list of test case fields, which field should hold this entry?

en: Expected Result
Comments
Test data
Assumptions
Unit to test

explanation.en: The article's field list describes Test data as "variables and their values", which is exactly what this entry is. Unit to test describes what is to be verified, and Expected Result holds the response the test should produce.

prompt.en: In the article's basic test case statement format "Verify ... Using ... With ... To ...", what does the "Using" part identify?

en: What is returned, shown or demonstrated as the result
The conditions under which the check is carried out
The tester's name and the timestamp of the execution
The priority of the test, such as high, medium or low
What is being tested, such as a tool name, tag name or dialog

explanation.en: Verify is the first word of the statement and Using names what is being tested ([tool name, tag name, dialog, etc.]); the article notes that "entering" or "selecting" may be used instead depending on the situation. Conditions belong to With, and what is returned or shown belongs to To.

source.section: Basic Format of Test Case Statement

prompt.en: A test case for an interest calculation simply says "enter any amount and check the interest", leaving the tester to pick the input values. Which tip from the article does this violate?

en: Review the test cases once as a tester
Bound as well as ease the testers
Prioritize the tests
Be a contributor
Never forget the end user

explanation.en: Tip #3 says testers should be given a range of inputs, especially where calculations are performed, instead of choosing the test data items themselves, and points to boundary value analysis. The review tip concerns dry-running finished cases, not supplying input ranges.

prompt.en: According to the article's tricks for excellent test documentation, which pair of test cases should be written for each scenario?

en: One UI case for the static fields and one database case for the stored credentials
One high-priority case for deadlines and one low-priority case for cosmetic checks
One positive case for the normal flow and one negative case for the exceptional flow
One manual case for new features and one automated case for the regression checks
One basic-flow case on a browser and one alternate-flow case on a mobile device

explanation.en: The trick "Do not forget to cover the negative cases" asks for two test cases per scenario: a positive one for the intended or normal flow and a negative one for the unintended or exceptional flow, because a negative case is as important as a positive case.

prompt.en: The article illustrates test prioritization with examples from a shopping website. Which assignment matches those examples?

en: Medium: denying access after an invalid login; High: showing relevant products
Medium: checking the color of button text; Low: showing relevant products
High: checking the color of button text; Low: denying access after an invalid login
High: denying access after an invalid login; Low: checking the color of button text
High: showing relevant products; Low: denying access after an invalid login

explanation.en: The article's examples are High for denying access after an invalid login attempt, Medium for showing relevant products on the user screen, and Low for checking the color of button text; under tight deadlines the high-priority tests are run first.

prompt.en: In a test for placing an online order, step (e) reads "Checkout and pay". Which problem from the article's "How NOT to write tests" section is this?

en: Composite step
Multiple conditions in one case
Missing negative case
Application behavior taken as expected behavior
Dependency conflict among test cases

explanation.en: "Checkout and pay" packs several actions into one step, which the article calls a composite step; it should be split into steps such as clicking Checkout, entering card, shipping and billing information, clicking Checkout and checking the confirmation page. Multiple conditions in one case means combining several scenarios, not several actions of one flow.

prompt.en: A tester writes the expected result for a shop's Shipping and Return page by copying what the page currently shows ("Put your info here" and a Continue button). What does the article recommend instead?

en: Tag the test as low priority because it only checks the displayed text
Split the expected result into atomic sub-steps for each displayed element
Write a separate test case for each element currently displayed on the page
Use the application only as a guide and write the researched intended behavior
Keep the copied result, since the running application is the most reliable source

explanation.en: Taking application behavior as expected behavior is risky because the application itself may be wrong; the article says to use the application only as a guide and write the correct intended behavior, e.g. that the order's shipping and return details are displayed after an order number is entered.

prompt.en: One login test contains these steps: (a) enter valid details and click Submit, (b) leave Username empty and click Submit, (c) leave Password empty and click Submit. Besides one failure marking the whole test as failed, what problem does the article point out?

en: After step (a) succeeds the user is logged in, so step (b) cannot proceed
Steps (b) and (c) need test data with the maximum allowed 30 characters
The expected results are copied from the application's current behavior
Steps (b) and (c) are positive cases and each need a matching negative case
Step (a) is a composite step that should be split into atomic sub-steps

explanation.en: With multiple conditions in one case the flow breaks: once step (a) logs the user in, the login option is no longer available for step (b). The article's fix is modular tests with one condition per test case, copying the shared steps where needed.

prompt.en: Among the documents the article says to collect before writing tests, which one is marked as OPTIONAL?

en: Functional Requirements Document
Software Project Plan
Business Use Case Document
User Requirements Document
QA/Test Plan

explanation.en: The article lists five documents: User Requirements Document, Business Use Case Document, Functional Requirements Document, Software Project Plan (Optional) and QA/Test Plan. Only the project plan, which covers objectives, priorities, milestones, schedule, risks and dependencies, is marked optional.

prompt.en: Which document from the article's collection list details scenarios from a business perspective, including actors, goals, pre- and post-conditions, basic and alternate flows, options and exceptions?

en: Functional Requirements Document
QA/Test Plan
Business Use Case Document
Software Project Plan
User Requirements Document

explanation.en: The article describes the Business Use Case Document as detailing use-case scenarios from a business perspective with actors, goals, conditions, flows, options and exceptions. The User Requirements Document instead covers business processes, user profiles and functional and non-functional requirements, and the QA/Test Plan covers standards, change control and acceptance criteria.

prompt.en: In the article's login-screen example, clicking the "Forgot Password?" link may email the user, so the email must be tested for the proper process and confirmation. Which category of cases from the example does this belong to?

en: Functional cases
Database cases
UI tests
Alternate-flow cases
Process tests

explanation.en: Process tests cover the processes associated with a feature rather than the actions of the visible controls, and the article uses the Forgot Password email as its example. Functional cases cover clicking dynamic controls such as the link itself, and UI tests cover the visible fields.

prompt.en: Applying the BAOE mantra to the login screen, clicking "Logout" after logging in (or a session timeout returning to the login screen) is an example of which element?

en: Boundaries
Alternate Flow
Options
Exceptions
Basic Flow

explanation.en: BAOE stands for Basic Flow, Alternate Flow, Options and Exceptions, each applied to positive and negative tests. For login, the basic flow is logging in through a browser, the alternate flow is logging in on a mobile device, options are logout or session timeout, and exceptions are wrong credentials giving an error message.

prompt.en: In the article's login test case document, one row enters the maximum allowed text in the User Name and Password boxes. What is the expected behaviour?

en: An alert "User Name and Password are Mandatory" should appear
The boxes should accept the maximum allowed 10 characters
The text should be refused, as it is not allowed in Registration
A "Session Expired" alert should appear and both boxes be cleared
The boxes should accept the maximum allowed 30 characters

explanation.en: The maximum-length row expects the fields to accept the maximum allowed 30 characters. Refusal because the text is not allowed in Registration is expected for input starting with special characters or blank spaces, and the Session Expired alert belongs to the 10-minute idle test.

prompt.en: Which of the following is one of the article's reasons for reusing test cases across web projects?

en: Most projects are enhancements or changes to existing functionality
Reused test cases no longer need to cover negative scenarios
Browser compatibility and security testing differ for every site
Each retail website has functional areas found on no other site
Web-based projects are rarely subject to requirement changes

explanation.en: The article's reasons include recurring functional areas (login, registration, cart, checkout), most projects being enhancements of existing functionality, frequent requirement changes in web projects and recurring test types such as browser compatibility, performance and security testing; the distractors contradict these points.

prompt.en: A tester adapts a standard test case from an earlier retail website for a new one. According to the article, how should the steps that must change per project be handled?

en: Merge them into one composite step to keep the test short
Highlight them in a different color for quick find-and-replace
Tag them as low priority so that they are executed last
Delete them and write those parts from scratch for each project
List them on the separate "Bugs" sheet of the workbook

explanation.en: Among its guidelines for a standard test, the article says to highlight modifiable steps in a different color so they can be found and replaced quickly; the author also used color-coding so reviewers could focus on the changed parts.
